title: Agentic Security: Permissions, Provenance, and the Agent Supply Chain — Steve Yegge, Gas Town
talk_summary: Steve Yegge argues that AI-generated code will multiply security defects and that security must be a dedicated, repeated pass rather than bundled with correctness. He recommends giving agents security tooling (SAST, supply-chain scanners) as explicit passes, running multiple review passes, and supervising 24/7 agents adversarially with least-privilege credentials.

takeaways.technique: Separate security pass from correctness pass
takeaways.what_they_do: Run security as its own dedicated agent pass after the code is functionally correct, rather than asking one prompt to do both.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can't give them security at the same time as you give them correctness. They'll do a half-ass job of both.

takeaways.what_they_do: Have the model review its own work up to 4-5 times (draft, revise, polish) because single-pass output is never ship-ready.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you have to get them to do up to four to five reviews of the work that they did before it's like actually ready to ship.

takeaways.technique: Give agents security scanners as tools
takeaways.what_they_do: Wire SAST/dependency/supply-chain scanners into the agent's toolset so it runs them as a final prompt step and cross-checks tools against each other.
takeaways.evidence_quote: have them run your security analysis, all of the tools... and have them check each other's work, too.
takeaways.numbers: 241 vulnerabilities found by scanner that the LLM hardening pass missed

takeaways.what_they_do: Treat hallucinated package names as an attack surface; verify every dependency the agent adds actually exists and is legitimate before install.
takeaways.evidence_quote: what it downloaded was a backdoor. Because that graphy123 wasn't a real package

takeaways.what_they_do: Run dedicated adversarial/supervisor agents over long-running queue-processing agents because one agent will eventually screw up.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I think of adversarial groups of agents tasked with doing that queue management cuz one agent will always eventually screw it up.

takeaways.what_they_do: Audit service-account credentials and split out permissions so each agent/action only has what it needs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: do they really need all those credentials on that service account? Really, right? Only for this one action, maybe we can like separate this one out.
